wall_texts.institution: Tate Modern (Performer and Participant display, Room 7), London
wall_texts.work: Britto Arts Trust, Rasad, 2024 (room text, about 210 words, 4 short paragraphs, plus a one-line standfirst)
structure: Standfirst (a headline under the title) states the claim in one line: the object, how many things, and the topic they comment on (hundreds of handmade sculptures, politics of food).
Sentence 1 gives title and year in italics, names the form (an installation) and its source of inspiration (the architecture of Bangladeshi markets).

Sentences 2-3 describe form and material in plain physical terms: a small bazaar, corrugated metal walls, slanted roofs, handmade replica foods in metal, ceramic and fabric. A small surprising detail follows (some bowls hold real spices).

Paragraph 2 hands the voice to the artists with a block quotation ('Britto Arts Trust writes: ...'), then lists specific objects in the work that carry slogans or jokes (razors, bomb-shaped bottles, fish-guns).
Paragraph 3 opens with a word-meaning move (the Bengali word means food, but also nourishment, knowledge, memory). It then states process (workshops, market visits, pottery sessions).
Paragraph 3 ends with the interpretive claim: the work 'considers' how globalised food economies affect communities, labour and natural resources in Bangladesh and beyond.
Last paragraph is a mini bio of the collective: founded where and when, artist-run, committed to the social, political and cultural realities of a country.
wall_texts.one_quote: Some of the bowls contain real spices and pulses.

wall_texts.institution: Tate Modern (Media Networks display, Room 7), London
wall_texts.work: Raimond Chaves, El Toque Criollo, 2003-7 (room text, about 165 words, 2 paragraphs, plus a question as standfirst)
structure: Standfirst is a question: 'What histories are revealed through album covers?'
Sentence 1 is an origin anecdote with a year and a place: the artist finds an object at a flea market in Lima.
Sentences 2-3 give facts that tie the find to the artist's family (his uncle's record label in Colombia).
Sentence 4 turns the anecdote into a method: an ongoing search through second-hand markets across Latin America, the Caribbean and the US.
Sentence 5 gives an artist quotation about his selection logic (cover images matter more than the music).
Paragraph 2 sentence 1 names the work and describes display logic: collected sleeves shown with the artist's commentary and lyric or speech excerpts.

Paragraph 2 sentence 2 counts the structure (19 groupings) and then gives a list of subjects the narrative addresses (migration, inequality, gender politics, drug trafficking, guerrilla conflict, globalisation).
Final sentence is a second artist quotation that says the stories are inferred, not shown. This leaves the interpretive close to the artist.
wall_texts.one_quote: An image of his family featured on the record sleeve.

wall_texts.institution: Tate Modern (Media Networks display, Room 3), London
wall_texts.work: Shashi Bikram Shah, Royal Massacre Series, 2001 (room text, about 320 words, 5 paragraphs; individual wall labels dated February 2026 follow, each about 70-90 words)
structure: Standfirst states the theme in one long sentence: this display explores civil conflict, mourning and memory in works documenting a key moment in Nepali history.

Paragraph 1: sentence 1 sets the mood ('a time of shock, violence and political unrest'); sentence 2 names the series and the historical trigger (the 2001 royal assassination); sentence 3 states material (newspaper cuttings); sentence 4 states the political aftermath (monarchy abolished, republic founded in 2008).
Paragraph 2 describes the object as a physical thing: what is on the front, what is on the back, which image repeats, how drawing is layered over clippings.
Paragraph 2 closes with a 'themes' sentence: Hindu motifs and mythological references blended with Nepali iconography, 'exploring themes of grief, politics and spirituality'.

Paragraph 3 justifies the material choice ('The choice of newspaper ... is particularly significant'): curfew, newspaper as the only information source, delivered to the artist's home, family ties to the monarchy and to paper manufacturing.

Paragraph 4 (final) places the work in the artist's practice and in the museum collection: the only works using collage and portraiture; first body of work by a Nepali artist to enter Tate's collection.

Individual wall labels in the same room: 1) what is depicted, 2) one iconographic detail explained (sword, snake god), 3) what the detail symbolises, 4) sometimes a long artist quotation, then the dated credit line 'Gallery label, February 2026'.
wall_texts.one_quote: Each drawing can be looked at from both sides.

wall_texts.institution: Tate Modern (Performer and Participant display, Room 5), London
wall_texts.work: Danica Dakić, ISOLA BELLA, 2007-8 (room text, about 200 words, 4 paragraphs plus an artist epigraph; a long single-paragraph artwork label of about 300 words sits below it)
structure: Standfirst is a one-line scene description: an imaginary island film set, participants, improvised performances developed with the artist.
Artist epigraph (block quotation) states the concept in the artist's own words: a paradise with no trace of people, linked to a socially isolated place.
Paragraph 1 states what is in the room, as an inventory: single-channel video, paper masks, handwritten notes, three posters, a photograph.
Paragraph 2 gives process and numbers (40 participants), plus the source image (a 19th-century panoramic wallpaper) and the origin of the title.
Paragraph 3 gives the site (a residential care home in a Bosnian village), the date range of the war, and how isolation affected the home.
Paragraph 4 describes the collaboration in verbs of care (worked closely, created a stage) and ends on what the participants gained (a chance to step into a utopian 'Isola Bella' on film).

A closing biography sentence gives where the artist lives and the stock phrase for her practice: works with communities to explore 'identity, belonging, cultural memory and history'. The longer label below delivers the same facts as one dense paragraph in neutral descriptive past and present tense.
wall_texts.one_quote: Titled Isola Bella ('beautiful island' in Italian), the wallpaper inspired Dakić's work.

wall_texts.institution: Tate Modern (Performer and Participant display, Room 6), London
wall_texts.work: Samson Kambalu, five 'Nyau cinema' videos (room text, about 150 words, 3 short paragraphs)
structure: Standfirst names the artist, the form (short improvised videos) and the artist's own term for it ('Nyau cinema') in quotation marks.

Paragraph 1 opens with the artist's surname (no first name after the heading), says how many works are in the room and where they were made, then explains the social purpose (a way to interact with other people).
Paragraph 1 describes the method (strangers film him, results posted on social media) and ends with an art-historical comparison (affinity with early silent comedy).
Paragraph 2 gives the rules the artist set himself (duration, acting style, audience engagement), then biographical context (childhood in 1980s Malawi, projectionists who re-edited films).
Paragraph 3 explains the key term ('Nyau cinema' relates to Chewa masking, performance and play).
Final sentence is an artist quotation about improvisation and taking Malawi everywhere. A sponsor credit line follows.
wall_texts.one_quote: Creating these scenes was a way for him to interact with other people.

wall_texts.institution: Tate Modern (Performer and Participant display, Room 8), London
wall_texts.work: Sovereignty of Quiet (display intro, about 70 words, 2 paragraphs; on view until 14 March 2027 per the page)
structure: Standfirst (one sentence) defines the group: US artists, depicting Black figures, in moments of repose or reflection, in domestic, private or imagined spaces of safety.
Sentence 1 introduces a writer and a concept via a short quotation ('quiet' as a metaphor for the full range of one's inner life).
Sentence 2 names the source book with year and subtitle and says the display takes it 'as its starting point'. It states the display's job: it explores 'quiet' as a form of expression.
The room is therefore built on one theory text, named in sentence 2. The rest of the meaning sits in the object labels.
wall_texts.one_quote: this display explores 'quiet' as a form of expression

wall_texts.institution: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York (Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing, 'Art & Artists' entries)
wall_texts.work: Eddie Rodolfo Aparicio, amber sculpture (about 204 words, one paragraph, work title not shown in the markdown text)
structure: Sentence 1 states the material first: 'This work is made primarily from' modified amber, with a gloss (a petrified form of tree resin).
Sentence 2 gives the artist's own words about why the material (it moves nutrients and heals wounds, in a tree).
Sentence 3 gives the material's history (jewellery, carved royalty and deities) and contrasts it with what this artist does with it.
Sentence 4 offers a theoretical reframe: the artist treats amber as an archive that refuses completion and fixity.
Sentences 5-6 list what is embedded in the amber (found pigeon wings, branches, clothing, documents of white activists' solidarity efforts) and the issue this raises (privilege and solidarity).
Sentence 7 explains behaviour over time: the amber is not fully rigid, so the sculpture will change shape during the exhibition because of gravity and light.
Final sentence converts the physical fact into metaphor: objects will move, suggesting how memory and trauma are held in the body and shift over time.
wall_texts.one_quote: This work is made primarily from modified amber, a petrified form of tree resin.

wall_texts.institution: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York (Whitney Biennial 2024)
wall_texts.work: Charisse Pearlina Weston, smoked-glass installation (about 181 words, one paragraph)
structure: Sentence 1 begins 'In this installation' and uses the artist's surname as subject. It describes the act (wedging large smoked-glass panes against the walls) and the effect ('a moment of pause before collapse, suspension, and heightened risk').
Sentence 2 gives the artist's second discipline (poet) and a cultural tradition (the Blues, repetition used to amplify meaning).
Sentence 3 turns the tradition into a literal practice: she reuses glass from a 2022 Queens Museum show.
Sentences 4-5 supply a historical research source (a planned 1964-65 'stall-in' by CORE chapters against the New York World's Fair, never executed) and how the earlier installation echoed it.
Sentence 6 delivers the key concept in the artist's own term ('tactics of Black refusal') and sets it against the usual meaning of glass (transparency and access).
Final sentence widens to a claim about art as an unresolved object: it evolves, makes new meanings and evades structures of ownership.

wall_texts.institution: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York (Whitney Biennial 2024)
wall_texts.work: Ligia Lewis, A Plot, A Scandal (about 114 words, one paragraph)
structure: Sentence 1 states where and how the film was made (shot in the historic quarters of Rimini) and the artist's critical reading of the site, in her own words ('Eurocentric ideals' of dominion over the land).
Sentence 2 gives one concrete example from the landscape (cypress trees in ordered rows) and calls it an 'example'.
Sentence 3 describes the film's opening (the sound of a church bell, later seen as a monument) and links it to Christian ideals that preceded the Enlightenment.

Final sentence names the method and aim: weaving historical epics with political and mythical narratives, using spectacle and scandal to address the dispossession of 'Europe's Others', a term attributed to the artist.
wall_texts.one_quote: filmed A Plot, A Scandal in the historic quarters of Rimini, Italy

wall_texts.institution: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York (Whitney Biennial 2026)
wall_texts.work: Kelly Akashi, Monument (Altadena), Inheritance (Distressed) and Imprints (about 110 words in 2 paragraphs, plus a bilingual English/Spanish object label for Imprints)
structure: Paragraph 1 sentence 1: the title in italics, then 'stands as a testament to' a public loss (the January 2025 Eaton Fire in Altadena).
Paragraph 1 sentence 2: the personal fact (her home and studio burned; only the chimney survived) and the making process (rebuilt piece by piece with a mason, in glass brick).
Paragraph 2 sentence 1: a second work, with its source object (a grandmother's doily, saved from a garage sale, then lost in the fire) and its material (cut into Cor-Ten steel).
Paragraph 2 sentence 2: an art-history note on the material (linked to Minimalism and to masculinity).
Final sentence is the thesis, in the generic 'explores' form: the work explores how artists, especially women, inherit and grapple with artistic and familial histories.
The object label for Imprints repeats the same facts in 2 sentences and ends on 'themes of familial inheritance and loss'.
wall_texts.one_quote: a testament to the widespread losses suffered in Altadena, California

wall_texts.institution: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
wall_texts.work: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing (exhibition overview text, about 290 words, 3 paragraphs plus credits)
structure: Paragraph 1 sentence 1: edition number, a claim about the institution ('longest-running survey of contemporary art in the United States'), number of artists, and the verb 'grappling with' today's pressing issues.

Paragraph 1 sentence 2: a metaphor for the viewer's experience, borrowed from an artist ('dissonant chorus'), with the formula 'provocative yet intimate' and 'probe the cracks and fissures of the unfolding moment'.
Paragraph 2 explains the title: it acknowledges that AI is complicating what is real and that rhetoric about gender and authenticity is used politically.

Paragraph 2 then names a long history (people deemed 'less than real') and states a curatorial commitment (amplify voices of artists confronting these legacies; provide a space where difficult ideas can be engaged).

Paragraph 3 lists the themes in one sentence (permeability of mind and body, fluidity of identity, precariousness of natural and constructed worlds) and lists methods (subversive humour, expressive abstraction, non-Western cosmological thinking).
Paragraph 3 ends in hope: pathways, strategies of coping and healing, and ways to come together 'even in a fractured time'. Credits follow (curators, then performance and film programme organisers).

wall_texts.work: Critical Fabulation (collection installation curated by Simone Leigh, Gallery 289, Oct 2025 - Jan 2026; about 250 words of running text between captions)
structure: Sentence 1 introduces the curating artist (Chicago-born, 'internationally renowned') and what she did (brought together works from African, American and European collections to explore relationships between objects).
Sentence 2 states the problem with museum display (chronology, geography and media separate overlapping stories).
Sentence 3 describes the artist's own practice (draws from African and African diasporic traditions) and names the theory source of the title (a cultural historian, Saidiya Hartman).
Sentence 4 states process (collaboration with museum curators) and then poses three direct questions: who determines significance, what deserves to be presented, how African objects are valued today.
Sentence 5 is a long list of named objects and artists placed together (pilgrim staffs, gold weights, twin figures, Brancusi, Hesse, Mendieta, McQueen, Picasso, Saar).
Sentence 6 interprets the juxtapositions as relationships that 'may reflect, or obscure' African aesthetic influence.
Final sentences invite the visitor to stage their own encounters, then give a curator credit line. Image captions in between name 3-4 artworks each with year.
wall_texts.one_quote: Who determines the significance of historical and cultural objects?

wall_texts.work: Made in L.A. 2025 (exhibition introduction, about 120 words, 1 paragraph)
structure: Sentence 1 states the edition (seventh iteration of the signature biennial) and the geographic scope (artists practising throughout greater Los Angeles).
Sentence 2 states the number of participants (28) and the criterion: work not only made in the city but grounded in its complex and unfolding terrain.
Sentence 3 is a sharp, balanced aphorism about the city ('Neither myth nor monolith ...', dissonance is its distinguishing feature).
Sentence 4 lists media in one run (film, painting, theater, choreography, photography, sculpture, sound, video).
Sentence 5 gives a colon sentence: a one-word thesis ('Attitude draws them together') then 'each engages with this city in ways alternately literal, formal, material, and metaphoric'.
Final sentence is a short closing line of belonging: conceived or made in Los Angeles, they are of this city and nowhere else. Curators, audioguide and funders follow.
wall_texts.one_quote: Conceived or made in Los Angeles, they are of this city and nowhere else.

wall_texts.work: An Indigenous Present (exhibition text, 2025-26, about 170 words in 3 paragraphs plus artist list)
structure: Sentence 1 names the exhibition and its type ('a thematic exhibition spanning 100 years of contemporary Indigenous art').

Sentence 2 gives counts (15 artists, new commissions) and the shared strategy: abstraction used to represent personal and collective narratives, describe real and imagined places, and build on cultural and aesthetic traditions.
Sentence 3 names the co-organisers and calls the show 'an expansive consideration' that highlights a continuum of elders and emerging makers. It names three newly commissioned artists.

Paragraph 2 gives the origin: the show grows from a 2023 publication of the same name. It states what the collaborative process produced and what the show demonstrates (the variability of abstraction and its capacity to hold multiple forms and histories).

Paragraph 3 lists public programmes (installation, performances of scores, film series). A tour sentence with venues and dates closes the section. Artist list follows, each with nation and birth place.
wall_texts.one_quote: An Indigenous Present is a thematic exhibition spanning 100 years of contemporary Indigenous art.

wall_text_vocabulary: Frame verbs found in the texts read: explores / exploring (the most common; Tate Shah, Tate Sovereignty of Quiet, Whitney Akashi, Whitney overview, AIC), draws on / draws from (Whitney Weston, AIC), addresses (Chaves), considers (Britto), engages with (Hammer), grapples with / grappling with (Whitney), probe (Whitney overview), highlights (Whitney, ICA), brings together (AIC, Tate), anchors (AIC), builds on (Serpentine press text read separately; ICA 'build upon'), reflects on (Whitney Akashi label), poses questions (AIC), prompts (AIC), invites (AIC).

Description verbs are plain and physical: made from, constructed from, displays, features, arranged in, layered with, embedded, wedged, repurposes, reuses, rebuilt, filmed, collected, inspired by, derived from.

Claim verbs that suggest a symbolic reading, usually in the last sentence: suggesting, symbolising, hints at, points to, evoking (Whitney Weston), stands as a testament to (Whitney Akashi), 'speak to'.

Nouns of theme (high frequency): memory (Aparicio, Shah, Britto), cultural memory, identity, belonging, migration, social inequality, labour, natural resources, globalisation, grief, mourning, trauma, loss, inheritance, dispossession, erasure, solidarity, privilege, refusal, legacies, archive, collaboration, community, resistance, utopia, mass media.

Nouns of material and form: installation, single-channel video, collage, newspaper cuttings, replica, stalls, wallpaper, amber, glass, steel, textile, recycled local materials, handmade, found materials, sleeves, archive.

Theory is cited by naming a person plus a book or phrase, not by jargon: a writer (Kevin Quashie, The Sovereignty of Quiet), a cultural historian (Saidiya Hartman, as source of the title), an artist's own term ('Nyau cinema', 'tactics of Black refusal', 'Europe's Others'). The abstract nouns come from the quotation, not from the museum voice.
Hedging and balance words: 'not simply', 'alternately literal, formal, material, and metaphoric', 'may reflect, or obscure', 'a kind of archive' (Whitney Aparicio), 'albeit one that ...'.

Recurring stock phrases: 'a series of', 'in collaboration with', 'across [region]', 'both ... and ...', 'the first ... to enter the collection', 'for the first time', 'responds to', 'in the aftermath of', 'drawing attention to', 'has noted', 'describes as', 'what she calls'.

NOT found in these 14 texts (so use sparingly, they are more typical of press releases and reviews): 'interrogates', 'unfolds', 'navigates', 'entanglement', 'liminal', 'rhizomatic', 'infrastructure'. These terms still suit the satirical target, but the real wall texts read here mostly use plainer verbs.
Titles of works are in italics with year; artist is named by surname after the first full-name mention. Collectives are named as 'the artist-run collective' with founding city and year.
wall_text_rules: Length: individual artwork or artist entries run about 100-200 words (Whitney 2024: 114, 181, 204). Room and display texts at Tate run about 70-320 words in 2-5 short paragraphs. Introductions to whole exhibitions run about 120-290 words in 1-3 paragraphs.

Structure of a room or display text at Tate: a one-line standfirst under the title (a claim, a scene description, or a question), then 2-5 short paragraphs of about 40-80 words, then a one-line credit or supporter note. The standfirst is a complete sentence with no final full stop in some cases.
The standfirst often takes one of three forms: 'This display explores X in a series of works ...', 'These [objects] display/comment on Y', or a question ('What histories are revealed through ...?').

Tense: present tense for what the work does and what is in the room ('the work takes the form of', 'Chaves displays'). Past tense for how the work was made and for history ('worked closely', 'was filmed', 'was inspired by'). Present perfect for artist's ongoing practice ('has noted', 'has developed').

First sentence patterns: (a) title + form + source ('Rasad 2024 is an installation inspired by ...'); (b) material first ('This work is made primarily from ...'); (c) 'In this installation, [Surname] has ...'; (d) 'In 2002, [Name] stumbled across ...' (origin anecdote); (e) edition + claim + number for exhibition intros ('the seventh iteration ... 28 participants').

Artists are named by full name on first mention, surname only afterwards, often with a role phrase ('the Inuit/Haitian/Taino filmmaker, writer, and activist'; 'a poet as well as a visual artist'; 'Chicago-born, internationally renowned contemporary artist'). Collectives are named with a founding place and year. Pronouns follow the artist's preference ('she', 'he', 'they') after the first mention.

Sentence length mixes: most sentences run 15-30 words. The closing sentence is often 20-40 words and carries the interpretive claim with a participle chain (suggesting..., exploring..., highlighting...). Short sentences (under 10 words) appear for a concrete surprise or a turn ('Some of the bowls contain real spices and pulses.', 'Each drawing can be looked at from both sides.').

Typical sentence order for an artwork text: (1) what it is and what it is made of; (2) a source or research fact (an archive, a historical event, a book, a place); (3) the artist's own words in a short quotation; (4) a process or material detail (how it was made, how it will change); (5) a theme sentence in a participle or 'explores' form; (6) sometimes a wider claim about practice or about art itself.

Quotation is used heavily: one or two short artist quotations per text, introduced by 'has noted', 'describes as', 'what she calls', 'writes'. Block quotations appear as epigraphs at Tate. Quotations carry the abstract language; the museum voice stays plain.

Rhetorical questions appear in about 1 in 5 texts (standfirst questions at Tate; a triple question in the AIC text). The Whitney and Hammer texts close on a claim, not a question. The AIC text closes on an invitation to the visitor.

Facts that give credibility: years, counts (40 participants, 19 groupings, 28 participants, 15 artists), named places, named institutions, named historical events and the date of the source material. A fictional generator should copy this habit and put one number and one place in every text.

Description of materials is physical and specific (corrugated metal, smoked glass, Cor-Ten steel, amber, newspaper cuttings) and usually includes at least one surprising ordinary object (pigeon wings, discarded clothing, real spices, doilies).
Credit lines: 'Gallery label, [Month Year]' at Tate for labels; curator and organiser names at the end of exhibition intros at Whitney, Hammer, ICA and AIC; sponsor line at Tate display level.

Tone: serious, caring, historically anchored, almost never ironic. Value words are 'significant', 'expressive', 'delicate', 'monumental', 'distinguishing'. Political content is stated directly (colonialism, dispossession, transphobia, Windrush) and attached to a named event or text.

Source limitations: moma.org and the Southbank Centre site (Hayward) returned HTTP 403; guggenheim.org served only a cookie banner; labiennale.org, sharjahart.org and serpentinegalleries.org pages read were press texts, not wall texts, so they were not used as wall-text examples. Tate display texts are current room texts (2024-2026 displays) for works that are older than 2023. The Sovereignty of Quiet display text is dated by the page as running to March 2027.
